claim: Group 1 innate lymphoid cells (G1-ILCs), including circulating natural killer (NK) cells and tissue-resident type 1 ILCs (ILC1s), are innate immune sentinels critical for responses against infection and cancer.
source: Group 1 innate lymphoid cells (G1-ILCs), including circulating natural killer (NK) cells and tissue-resident type 1 ILCs (ILC1s), are innate immune sentinels critical for responses against infection and cancer.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about the role of G1-ILCs in immunity.

claim: Diverse ILC1 subsets have been characterized across and within tissues in mice.
source: In contrast to relatively uniform NK cells through the body, diverse ILC1 subsets have been characterized across and within tissues in mice, but their developmental and functional heterogeneity remain unsolved.
evidence: This statement references existing characterization of ILC1 diversity in the literature.

claim: Liver parenchymal niches support the development of a cytotoxic ILC1 subset lacking IL-7 receptor (7R− ILC1s).
source: Here, using multimodal in vivo approaches including fate-mapping and targeting of the interleukin 15 (IL-15)-producing microenvironment, we demonstrate that liver parenchymal niches support the development of a cytotoxic ILC1 subset lacking IL-7 receptor (7 R− ILC1s).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from fate-mapping and IL-15 niche targeting experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Fetal liver (FL) G1-ILCs arise perivascularly and then differentiate into 7R− ILC1s within sinusoids during ontogeny.
source: During ontogeny, fetal liver (FL) G1-ILCs arise perivascularly and then differentiate into 7 R− ILC1s within sinusoids.
evidence: This developmental trajectory is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data showing spatial localization patterns.

claim: Hepatocyte-derived IL-15 supports parenchymal development of FL G1-ILCs to maintain adult pool of 7R− ILC1s.
source: Hepatocyte-derived IL-15 supports parenchymal development of FL G1-ILCs to maintain adult pool of 7 R− ILC1s.
evidence: This is supported by data from Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice showing reduction in FL G1-ILCs and adult 7R− ILC1s.

claim: IL-7R+ (7R+) ILC1s in the liver are not essential for 7R− ILC1 development in physiological conditions.
source: IL-7R+ (7R+) ILC1s in the liver, candidate precursors for 7 R− ILC1s, are not essential for 7 R− ILC1 development in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments and age-dependent kinetics showing independent development of the two subsets.

claim: 7R− ILC1s exhibit killing activity at steady state through granzyme B expression.
source: Functionally, 7 R− ILC1s exhibit killing activity at steady state through granzyme B expression, which is underpinned by constitutive mTOR activity, unlike NK cells with exogenous stimulation-dependent cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assays, granzyme B expression data, and rapamycin treatment experiments.

claim: 7R− ILC1s have constitutive mTOR activity that underpins their granzyme B expression.
source: Functionally, 7 R− ILC1s exhibit killing activity at steady state through granzyme B expression, which is underpinned by constitutive mTOR activity, unlike NK cells with exogenous stimulation-dependent cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-S6 staining data and rapamycin treatment experiments showing mTOR-dependent granzyme B expression.

claim: Mouse ILC1s can be distinguished from NK cells by their CD49a+CD49b− phenotype, strict tissue-residency, and Eomes-independence.
source: In contrast, mouse ILC1s can be distinguished from NK cells by their CD49a+CD49b− phenotype, strict tissue-residency, and Eomes-independence (Daussy et al., 2014; Gasteiger et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2013; Sojka et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: ILC progenitors (ILCPs) expressing PLZF and/or PD-1 preferentially differentiate into ILC1s more than NK cells.
source: Additionally, ILC1s and NK cells are developmentally different in general, as confirmed by the fact that ILC progenitors (ILCPs) expressing PLZF and/or PD-1 as well as liver-resident Lin–Sca-1+Mac-1+ (LSM) and Lin–CD49a+CD122+ ILC1 precursors preferentially differentiate into ILC1s more than NK cells (Bai et al., 2021; Constantinides et al., 2015; Constantinides et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous developmental studies.

claim: NK cells are traditionally considered as more cytotoxic than ILC1s in mice.
source: In mice, NK cells are traditionally considered as more cytotoxic than ILC1s (Vivier et al., 2018), although this view has been questioned recently (Dadi et al., 2016; Kansler et al., 2022; Krabbendam et al., 2021; Nixon et al., 2022; Yomogida et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement references both traditional views and recent challenges to them through citations.

claim: Murine NK cells show low expression of cytotoxic molecules and only minimal cytotoxicity in their steady state.
source: Indeed, murine NK cells show low expression of cytotoxic molecules and only minimal cytotoxicity in their steady state (Fehniger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fehniger et al., 2007.

claim: The cytotoxicity of NK cells requires mTOR-dependent metabolic reprogramming mediated by cytokine signaling such as IL-15 or by NK receptor engagement.
source: The cytotoxicity of NK cells requires the mTOR-dependent metabolic reprogramming mediated by cytokine signaling such as IL-15 or by NK receptor engagement (Marçais et al., 2014; Nandagopal et al., 2014), but whether such cytotoxic machinery also exists in ILC1s is unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mechanistic studies.

claim: ILC1s can immediately respond and produce IFN-γ during liver injury.
source: By contrast, ILC1s can immediately respond and produce IFN-γ during liver injury (Nabekura et al., 2020) and virus infection (Weizman et al., 2017), highlighting the unique roles of ILC1s in the ignition of type 1 immunity in tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Liver ILC1s are separated into IL-7R-negative (7R−) and -positive (7R+) subsets.
source: Liver ILC1s are separated into IL-7R-negative (7 R−) and -positive (7R+) subsets (Friedrich et al., 2021; Sparano et al., 2022; Yomogida et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies characterizing ILC1 heterogeneity.

claim: G1-ILCs in the fetal liver (FL) are identified as precursors of ILC1s.
source: G1-ILCs in the fetal liver (FL) are identified as precursors of ILC1s (Chen et al., 2022; Sparano et al., 2022), especially of Ly-49E+ ILC1s that are included in 7 R− ILC1s (Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent developmental studies.

claim: 7R+ ILC1s in the liver, salivary glands (SG), and small intestines can give rise to 7R− ILC1s in response to cytokines and inflammations.
source: In addition, 7R+ ILC1s in the liver, salivary glands (SG), and small intestines can give rise to 7 R− ILC1s in response to cytokines and inflammations (Friedrich et al., 2021), suggesting that 7R+ ILC1s are also potential precursors for 7 R− ILC1s.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Friedrich et al., 2021.

claim: In ILC1-related inflammation models, ILC1s with high cytokine receptors (IL-7R, IL-18R, and/or CD25) are induced and accumulate in the liver.
source: In ILC1-related inflammation models reported so far, including contact hypersensitivity, MCMV infection, and liver injury, ILC1s with high cytokine receptors (IL-7R, IL-18R, and/or CD25) are induced and accumulate in the liver (Nabekura et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018; Weizman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple inflammation model studies.

claim: Liver 7R− ILC1s represent a unique population distinct from SG and small intestines based on organ-wide single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.
source: Furthermore, an organ-wide single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis reveals that liver 7 R− ILC1s represent a unique population distinct from SG and small intestines (McFarland et al., 2021), suggesting the absence of universal differentiation programs of ILC1s conserved across tissues.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McFarland et al., 2021.

claim: G1-ILC homeostasis heavily depends on interleukin 15 (IL-15).
source: G1-ILC homeostasis heavily depends on interleukin 15 (IL-15), that is transpresented from hematopoietic and stromal cells as an IL-15/IL-15Rα complex to locally promote the development, survival, and proliferation of memory CD8 T cells, NKT cells, and G1-ILCs in various tissues (Ikuta et al., 2021; Klose et al., 2014; Lodolce et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on IL-15 biology.

claim: FL G1-ILCs highly expressed CXCR6, TRAIL, and CD200R, resembling adult tissue ILC1s.
source: FL G1-ILCs highly expressed CXCR6, TRAIL, and CD200R, resembling adult tissue ILC1s, though they completely lacked IL-7R expression (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: FL G1-ILCs completely lacked IL-7R expression.
source: FL G1-ILCs highly expressed CXCR6, TRAIL, and CD200R, resembling adult tissue ILC1s, though they completely lacked IL-7R expression (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The frequencies and numbers of AL 7R− and 7R+ ILC1s were not reduced in Il7–/– mice.
source: Despite the differential IL-7R expression, the frequencies and numbers of AL 7 R− and 7R+ ILC1s were not reduced in Il7–/– mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B), consistent with the basic property of G1-ILCs of being IL-7-independent (Klose et al., 2014; Robinette et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Il7–/– mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: FL G1-ILCs and AL 7R− ILC1s shared high expression of ILC1 signature genes (P2rx7, Zfp683, and Cd3g) and low expression of NK cell signature genes (Sell, Klra4, and Klra8).
source: Consistent with surface phenotype, FL G1-ILCs and AL 7 R− ILC1s as well as BM iILC1s and AL 7R+ ILC1s shared high expression of ILC1 signature genes (P2rx7, Zfp683, and Cd3g) and low expression of NK cell signature genes (Sell, Klra4, and Klra8) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 7R+ ILC1s and BM iILC1s showed higher expression of genes related to cytokine responses (Il7r, Il2ra, Icos, and Kit) compared to other G1-ILC subsets.
source: By contrast, 7R+ ILC1s and BM iILC1s showed higher expression of genes related to cytokine responses (Il7r, Il2ra, Icos, and Kit) compared to other G1-ILC subsets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: FL G1-ILCs and 7R− ILC1s poorly expressed cytokine receptor-related genes (Il7r, Il18r1, and Il18rap).
source: Conversely, FL G1-ILCs and 7 R− ILC1s poorly expressed cytokine receptor-related genes (Il7r, Il18r1, and Il18rap) (Figure 1E) and exhibited less cytokine-responsive characters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and pathway analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed that the overall transcriptional state of FL G1-ILCs was close to 7R− ILC1s.
source: Although FL G1-ILCs were unique in terms of their high proliferative status (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G), principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that the overall transcriptional state of FL G1-ILCs was close to 7 R− ILC1s (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: FL G1-ILCs and AL 7R− ILC1s exhibited T-bet+Eomes− phenotype.
source: Given the ILC1-like transcriptional programs and T-bet+Eomes− phenotype of FL G1-ILCs and AL 7 R− ILC1s (Figure 1G), they were considered as ILC1s but not NK cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In PLZF fate-mapping experiments, AL 7R− and 7R+ ILC1s prominently expressed YFP.
source: In these chimeric mice, AL 7 R− and 7R+ ILC1s as well as other adult tissue ILC1s prominently expressed YFP (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is supported by fate-mapping data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: FL G1-ILCs mostly expressed YFP in straight PLZF-fm mice.
source: Furthermore, FL G1-ILCs mostly expressed YFP in straight PLZF-fm mice (Figure 1J), in line with a previous fate-mapping study of neonatal liver G1-ILCs (Constantinides et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by fate-mapping data shown in Figure 1J and a citation to previous work.

claim: In the liver, while 7R+ ILC1s were nearly absent in infants and accumulated with age, 7R− ILC1s were predominant in young mice, decreased with age, and eventually depleted.
source: However, in the liver, while 7R+ ILC1s were nearly absent in infants and accumulated with age, 7 R− ILC1s were predominant in young mice, decreased with age, and eventually depleted (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by age-dependent kinetics data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: 7R+ ILC1s highly expressed RORα and were positively enriched with gene sets 'RORA activates gene expression' relative to 7R− ILC1s.
source: RNA-seq revealed that 7R+ ILC1s highly expressed RORα and were positively enriched with gene sets 'RORA activates gene expression' relative to 7 R− ILC1s, based on gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and GSEA data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 7R+ ILC1s were significantly reduced in Rora+/– mice, while NK cells and 7R− ILC1s were unchanged.
source: 7R+ ILC1s were significantly reduced in Rora+/– mice, while NK cells and 7 R− ILC1s were unchanged (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Rora+/– mice shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In Rora–/– mice, 7R+ ILC1s were the subset most apparently affected.
source: In Rora–/– mice, although whole ILC1s were significantly reduced in line with a recent study using Ncr1Cre and Vav1Cre Rorafl/fl mice (Song et al., 2021), 7R+ ILC1s were the subset most apparently affected (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Rora–/– mice shown in Figure 2F and a citation to Song et al., 2021.

claim: For at least 2 months, little conversion was observed between 7R− and 7R+ ILC1s in adoptive transfer experiments.
source: For at least 2 months, little conversion was observed between 7 R− and 7R+ ILC1s (Figure 2G–I), as evidenced by IL-7R and IL-18R1 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transferred BM iILC1s gave rise to AL 7R+ ILC1s but not to 7R− ILC1s.
source: In addition, transferred BM iILC1s gave rise to AL 7R+ ILC1s but not to 7 R− ILC1s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C), consistent with their transcriptional resemblance.
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Parabiosis experiments showed that the replacement rate of AL 7R+ ILC1s were low (<5%), though significantly higher than that of 7R− ILC1s.
source: However, parabiosis experiments showed that the replacement rate of AL 7R+ ILC1s were low (<5%), though significantly higher than that of 7 R− ILC1s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that both ILC1 subsets are tissue-resident.
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s proliferated more than 7R− ILC1s after IL-15/IL-15Rα stimulation.
source: NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s proliferated more than 7 R− ILC1s after the stimulation (Figure 2J), consistent with their basal Ki-67 expression levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) and properties of cytokine responsiveness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 2J and references to previous figures.

claim: 7R− and 7R+ ILC1s were stable even after IL-15/IL-15Rα stimulation.
source: 7 R− and 7R+ ILC1s were stable even after the IL-15/IL-15Rα stimulation (Figure 2K), confirming their stability in activated states.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic stability data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Adoptively transferred FL G1-ILCs differentiated into CD49a+CD49blo mature ILC1s in AL and they completely lacked IL-7R.
source: Adoptively transferred FL G1-ILCs differentiated into CD49a+CD49blo mature ILC1s in AL (Figure 3A) and they completely lacked IL-7R (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: In fate-mapping experiments using Ncr1-CreERT2 mice, tdTomato expression was clearly restricted to IL-7R− fractions within neonatal G1-ILCs and AL ILC1s.
source: After tamoxifen injection into pregnant mice at E17.5, liver of neonatal and 4 weeks old pups were analyzed. TdTomato expression was clearly restricted to IL-7R− fractions within neonatal G1-ILCs and AL ILC1s (Figure 3C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), consistent with previous studies (Chen et al., 2022; Sparano et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by fate-mapping data shown in Figure 3C–E and citations to previous studies.

claim: Labeling efficiency was 40% in neonatal IL-7R− G1-ILCs and 20% in 7R− ILC1s in 4 weeks old mice in fate-mapping experiments.
source: Labeling efficiency was 40% in neonatal IL-7R− G1-ILCs and 20% in 7 R− ILC1s in 4 weeks old mice (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by fate-mapping data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: In E18.5 liver, FL G1-ILCs mostly distributed at perivascular sites, outside of the sinusoidal lumen (parenchyma).
source: In E18.5 liver, FL G1-ILCs mostly distributed at perivascular sites, outside of the sinusoidal lumen (here termed parenchyma; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Over 85% of whole ILC1s and NK cells were within sinusoids in AL.
source: In contrast, over 85% of whole ILC1s and NK cells were within sinusoids in AL (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 4B and quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: FCM-based analysis of intravenous CD45.2 staining confirmed similar intravascular locations of 7R− and 7R+ ILC1s as well as NK cells, T cells, and NKT cells in AL.
source: Although we could not detect IL-7R expression on ILC1s by immunofluorescence, flow cytometry (FCM)-based analysis of intravenous (i.v.) CD45.2 staining confirmed similar intravascular locations of 7 R− and 7R+ ILC1s as well as NK cells, T cells, and NKT cells in AL (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by i.v. staining data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: ILC2s were not efficiently labeled by i.v. staining, consistent with perivascular localization of liver ILC2s.
source: In contrast, ILC2s were not efficiently labeled by i.v. staining, consistent with perivascular localization of liver ILC2s observed so far (Dahlgren et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by i.v. staining data shown in Figure 4E and a citation to Dahlgren et al., 2019.

claim: A population of AL Lin–Sca-1+Mac-1+ (LSM) cells were not well labeled by i.v. staining.
source: Interestingly, a population of AL Lin–Sca-1+Mac-1+ (LSM) cells, local precursors for ILC1s (Bai et al., 2021), were also not well labeled by i.v. staining.
evidence: This is supported by i.v. staining data shown in Figure 4E and a citation to Bai et al., 2021.

claim: Reanalysis of single nuclei RNA-seq data of whole liver cells revealed that Il15 gene was highly expressed by macrophages and endothelial cells and, to a lesser extent, by hepatocytes.
source: Reanalysis of single nuclei RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) data of whole liver cells from Liver Cell Atlas (https://www.livercellatlas.org/) revealed that Il15 gene was highly expressed by macrophages and endothelial cells and, to a lesser extent, by hepatocytes, while Il15ra expression was prominent in hepatocytes (Figure 5A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Il15ra expression was prominent in hepatocytes based on snRNA-seq data.
source: Reanalysis of single nuclei RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) data of whole liver cells from Liver Cell Atlas (https://www.livercellatlas.org/) revealed that Il15 gene was highly expressed by macrophages and endothelial cells and, to a lesser extent, by hepatocytes, while Il15ra expression was prominent in hepatocytes (Figure 5A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice, FL G1-ILCs were significantly reduced.
source: To target parenchymal IL-15, we generated Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice, which lacked IL-15 in hepatocytes. In Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice, FL G1-ILCs were significantly reduced (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice showed reduction of AL 7R− ILC1s in contrast to unchanged NK cells, 7R+ ILC1s, and NKT cells.
source: Notably, Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice also showed reduction of AL 7 R− ILC1s in contrast to unchanged NK cells, 7R+ ILC1s, and NKT cells (Figure 5D and E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), despite their similar intravascular localizations.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: In Lyve1Cre/+ Il15fl/fl mice, all AL G1-ILC subsets were significantly reduced.
source: In Lyve1Cre/+ Il15fl/fl mice, all AL G1-ILC subsets were significantly reduced (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Lyve1Cre/+ Il15fl/fl mice shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Lyz2-Cre Il15fl/fl mice showed similar two-fold reductions of AL NK cells, 7R− ILC1s, and 7R+ ILC1s.
source: Lyz2-Cre Il15fl/fl mice showed similar two-fold reductions of AL NK cells, 7 R− ILC1s, and 7R+ ILC1s (Figure 5G), confirming the similar IL-15 requirements among all G1-ILC subsets.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from Lyz2-Cre Il15fl/fl mice shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Expression of Bcl-2 was downregulated in all G1-ILCs of Lyve1Cre/+ Il15fl/fl mice.
source: Notably, expression of Bcl-2, a survival factor downstream of IL-15, was downregulated in all G1-ILCs of Lyve1Cre/+ Il15fl/fl mice (Figure 5H and I), whereas Bcl-2 and Ki-67 levels were unchanged in Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: Bcl-2 and Ki-67 levels were unchanged in Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice.
source: Notably, expression of Bcl-2, a survival factor downstream of IL-15, was downregulated in all G1-ILCs of Lyve1Cre/+ Il15fl/fl mice (Figure 5H and I), whereas Bcl-2 and Ki-67 levels were unchanged in Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice (Figure 5J and K).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5J and K.

claim: Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice had reduced Lin−CD122+CD49a+ ILC1 precursors in AL.
source: Alb-Cre Il15fl/fl mice had reduced Lin−CD122+CD49a+ ILC1 precursors in AL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), suggesting an impaired development of 7 R− ILC1s.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In steady state, minimal levels of granzyme B and death ligands were found on NK cells, while 7R− ILC1s expressed both granzyme B and TRAIL.
source: In steady state, minimal levels of granzyme B and death ligands were found on NK cells, while 7 R− ILC1s expressed both granzyme B and TRAIL, the latter of which was also expressed on 7R+ ILC1s (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B; Friedrich et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and B and supplementary figures.

claim: Freshly isolated 7R− ILC1s remarkably lysed multiple tumor cells including YAC-1, Hepa1-6, and B16F10 cells.
source: In line with this, freshly isolated 7 R− ILC1s remarkably lysed multiple tumor cells including YAC-1 (Figure 6C), Hepa1-6 (Figure 6D), and B16F10 cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 6C, D, and E.

claim: NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s showed only slight or no cytotoxicity against tumor cells.
source: By contrast, NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s showed only slight or no cytotoxicity against these tumor cells, consistent with a previous study showing minimal cytotoxicity of unstimulated NK cells (Fehniger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 6C, D, and E and a citation to Fehniger et al., 2007.

claim: Killing of Hepa1-6 cells by 7R− ILC1s was markedly inhibited by concanamycin A (CMA), and to a lesser extent by anti-TRAIL antibody.
source: Killing of Hepa1-6 cells by 7 R− ILC1s was markedly inhibited by CMA, and to a lesser extent by anti-TRAIL antibody (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data with inhibitors shown in Figure 6F.

claim: CMA had no effect on the cytotoxicity of NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s.
source: Despite the expression of granzyme A in NK cells and granzyme C in 7R+ ILC1s (Nixon et al., 2022; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D), CMA had no effect to their cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity assay data with CMA shown in Figure 6F and citations.

claim: Expression levels of granzyme B, as well as TRAIL and granzyme C, in each G1-ILC subset were clearly upregulated by in vitro stimulation of IL-15.
source: Expression levels of granzyme B, as well as TRAIL and granzyme C, in each G1-ILC subset were clearly upregulated by in vitro stimulation of IL-15 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) and in vivo injection of IL-15/IL-15Rα complex (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, and 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from IL-15 stimulation experiments shown in multiple figures.

claim: IL-15 stimulation and IL-15/IL-15Rα injection enhanced granzyme B more efficiently on NK cells than 7R− ILC1s.
source: Interestingly, however, both IL-15 stimulation and IL-15/IL-15Rα injection enhanced granzyme B more efficiently on NK cells than 7 R− ILC1s, and thereby the granzyme B levels of NK cells overwhelmed or got comparable to those of 7 R− ILC1s (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data comparing granzyme B induction shown in Figure 6A and supplementary figures.

claim: IL-15/IL-15Rα injection triggered the phosphorylation of STAT5, Akt, and ribosomal protein S6 in NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s but to a lesser degree in 7R− ILC1s.
source: IL-15/IL-15Rα injection also triggered the phosphorylation of STAT5, Akt, and ribosomal protein S6 (a target of mTOR), which are critical for the IL-15-induced effector function (Ali et al., 2015), in NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s but to a lesser degree in 7 R− ILC1s (Figure 6G and H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, and 1 G).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G and H and supplementary figures, and a citation to Ali et al., 2015.

claim: The phosphorylation level of S6 was rather higher in ILC1s than NK cells in unstimulated mice.
source: Interestingly, the phosphorylation level of S6 was rather higher in ILC1s than NK cells in unstimulated mice (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Injection of rapamycin downregulated granzyme B expression in 7R− ILC1s to a level comparable to that in NK cells.
source: Notably, injection of rapamycin, an mTOR complex inhibitor, downregulated granzyme B expression in 7 R− ILC1s to a level comparable to that in NK cells (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from rapamycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Granzyme B levels in NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s were unaffected by rapamycin.
source: By contrast, granzyme B levels in NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s were unaffected.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapamycin treatment data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: 7R− and 7R+ ILC1s behave like independent subsets under physiological conditions based on decline of 7R− ILC1s and accumulation of 7R+ ILC1s with age, requirements for RORα specifically in 7R+ ILC1s, and phenotypical stability between 7R− and 7R+ ILC1s when transferred into WT host mice.
source: However, we show that 7 R− and 7R+ ILC1s behave like independent subsets under physiological conditions: decline of 7 R− ILC1s and accumulation of 7R+ ILC1s with age, requirements for RORα specifically in 7R+ ILC1s, and phenotypical stability between 7 R− and 7R+ ILC1s when transferred into WT host mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: AL 7R+ ILC1s resemble 'memory-like' or 'activated' ILC1s in terms of the surface phenotype and high proliferation potentials.
source: AL 7R+ ILC1s resemble such 'memory-like' or 'activated' ILC1s in terms of the surface phenotype and high proliferation potentials.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with ILC1s described in inflammation models.

claim: Fate-mapping reveals that FL-derived 7R− ILC1s contain also an Ly49E/F− population (20–25%).

claim: One possible explanation for the local effect of hepatocyte-derived IL-15 is that the transpresentation of IL-15/IL-15Rα by hepatocytes may require direct contact to target cells, as dendritic cells do.

claim: It is possible that hepatocytes may produce IL-15Rα as a soluble form, that binds to other cell-derived IL-15 to exert non-local effects.
source: Given that hepatocytes prominently express Il15ra gene and its deletion results in the reduction of whole IL-15-dependent lymphocytes in the liver (Cepero-Donates et al., 2016), it is also possible that hepatocytes may produce IL-15Rα as a soluble form, that binds to other cell-derived IL-15 to exert non-local effects.
evidence: This is a speculation about IL-15Rα function, with a citation to Cepero-Donates et al., 2016.

claim: The age of mice selected for analysis influences the composition and overall cytotoxicity of ILC1s.
source: First, the age of mice selected for analysis influence the composition and overall cytotoxicity of ILC1s. We and others (Chen et al., 2022; Friedrich et al., 2021; Nixon et al., 2022) showed that ILC1s were heterogenous in their cytotoxicity. Due to the age-dependent reduction of highly cytotoxic 7 R− ILC1s, the overall cytotoxicity of ILC1s in the liver should decline with age.
evidence: This is an inference based on the age-dependent changes in ILC1 composition and citations to other studies.

claim: 7R− ILC1s are 'ready-to-kill' sentinels that contribute to the tonic immune surveillance, which is followed later by the response of activated and proliferated NK cells and 7R+ ILC1s.
